terms.definition: The ranking of Bordeaux wines prepared by the city's wine brokers for the 1855 Exposition Universelle in Paris, based on trading prices. It lists 61 red wines (60 from the Médoc plus Haut-Brion in Graves) in five growths and 27 sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac. Changes have been rare: Cantemerle was added in September 1855 and Mouton Rothschild was promoted to first growth in 1973. Estates that changed size or quality kept their rank.

Adding acid, usually tartaric, to must or wine to raise acidity, common in warm regions where grapes lose acid as they ripen, such as Australia, California and southern Europe. EU rules limit when and where it is allowed, and in principle it cannot be combined with chaptalisation on the same wine. Climate change has made acidification increasingly common in regions that once never needed it.

The brilliant white soil of the Jerez region, made of chalky marl rich in calcium carbonate and diatoms (fossil algae), deposited on an ancient seabed. It absorbs winter rain like a sponge, then forms a hard crust in summer that limits evaporation, letting vines survive the hot, dry season without irrigation. The best sherry pagos, such as Macharnudo, Carrascal and Balbaína, are on albariza.

Bush training in Italy ('little tree'), common in the south, Sicily and Sardinia. On Pantelleria, the head-trained vite ad alberello, planted in hollows to shelter it from the wind, was inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2014, the first agricultural practice to be listed. Etna also has many old alberello vineyards, some ungrafted, planted at high density.

A hard, pale, compact limestone-marl from the Eocene common in Chianti Classico, especially around Castellina, Castelnuovo Berardenga and Panzano. It breaks down into stony, calcareous soils that drain well and reflect light. Wines from alberese are often said to be broader and more powerful than those from galestro. Many Tuscan farmhouses are built of alberese blocks.

A fan-shaped deposit of gravel, sand and silt laid down where a stream leaves a canyon and spreads onto a plain. Alluvial fans drain well and have varied soils. Famous examples include the Rutherford Bench and Oakville in Napa Valley, Gimblett Gravels in Hawke's Bay and much of Mendoza. Cabernet Sauvignon from Napa's fans developed the reputation for 'Rutherford dust'.

Elevation strongly affects wine. Temperature falls by roughly 0.6 degrees Celsius per 100 metres, so high vineyards are cooler, with more sunlight intensity and larger diurnal ranges. Salta in Argentina has vineyards above 3,000 metres, and Swiss vineyards at Visperterminen reach about 1,100 metres. With climate change, growers in Europe and South America are planting higher to keep freshness.

A sherry that starts life under flor as a fino and then, when the flor dies or after refortification, continues ageing oxidatively. It combines fino's tangy, almond notes with oloroso's nutty, amber depth. Its name refers to Montilla, where the style may have originated. Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Cask of Amontillado' (1846) made it famous in literature.

A two-handled clay jar used by Greeks, Phoenicians and Romans to transport and store wine, often sealed with resin or pitch. Stamped handles reveal origin and date, so amphora finds map ancient wine trade routes. Today 'amphora wine' refers broadly to wine fermented or aged in clay vessels, including Georgian qvevri, Spanish tinajas, Portuguese talhas and modern Italian anfore.

Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée, the French appellation system created by a 1935 decree-law and managed by the INAO. Each AOC specifies its area (often down to the parcel), grape varieties, minimum ripeness, maximum yield, viticulture and winemaking methods. France has about 360 wine AOCs. Since 2009 the EU term AOP (Appellation d'Origine Protégée) may be used instead. The system protects names and traditions but has been criticised for rigidity.

Drying grapes after harvest to concentrate sugar and flavour, traditionally on bamboo racks or in lofts (fruttai) for three to four months in the Veneto. Grapes lose up to 40 percent of their weight. It is used for Amarone, Recioto della Valpolicella, Recioto di Soave, Sforzato di Valtellina and Vin Santo. The drying also changes the grape's chemistry, adding raisin, cherry and spice notes. Modern producers often use controlled drying rooms.

A legally defined geographical name for wine, with rules on boundaries and often on grape varieties, yields, alcohol and production methods. France's Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée (AOC), created in 1935, is the model. Within the EU, appellations are registered as Protected Designations of Origin (PDO). Outside Europe, the term often refers only to geography, as with American Viticultural Areas and Australian Geographical Indications, which do not regulate grapes or yields.

A local name on Santorini for the island's pumice-rich volcanic soil, formed after the Minoan eruption around 1600 BC. It is low in organic matter and contains almost no clay, so phylloxera never established itself, and vines grow on ungrafted roots that may be hundreds of years old. Aspa holds moisture from sea fog and dew, which is vital because the island receives very little rain.

Blending wines of different grape varieties, vineyards, vintages or barrels to create the final wine. It is central to Bordeaux, where château blends combine Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc, and to Champagne, where non-vintage cuvées blend dozens of base wines and reserve wines. The chef de cave or winemaker tastes the components in the spring after harvest to decide proportions.

Hungarian for individually picked, botrytis-shrivelled berries, and for Tokaji Aszú, the sweet wine made by soaking them in fermenting must or base wine. Traditionally the berries were collected in 20 to 25 litre hods (puttony) and measured by the number added to a 136 litre barrel (gönci). Since a 2013 reform, Tokaji Aszú must have at least 120 grams per litre of residual sugar, the old 5 puttonyos level, and the puttonyos figure has become optional.

Literally 'selected harvest', the third Prädikat, from selected very ripe bunches, often with some botrytis. Auslese is usually sweet and rich but can be dry. Some producers mark especially concentrated examples with gold capsules or stars, but these are private quality signals, not legal categories. Well-made Auslese from the Mosel or Rheingau can age for decades. Above it come Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.

American Viticultural Area, a federally recognised US grape-growing region defined by geographic features such as soil, climate and elevation, approved by the TTB (Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau). The first was Augusta, Missouri, in 1980. There are more than 270 AVAs. An AVA wine must contain at least 85 percent grapes from the area. Unlike European appellations, AVAs do not regulate grape varieties, yields or methods.

Aramon × Rupestris Ganzin No. 1, a rootstock bred in France in the 1870s with half vinifera ancestry. UC Davis recommended it widely in California from the 1960s, though French researchers had warned that it was not resistant enough. In the 1980s a new phylloxera strain (biotype B) attacked AXR1 vineyards in Napa and Sonoma, forcing growers to replant a large share of their vineyards in the 1990s, at enormous cost.

A dark volcanic rock formed from fast-cooling lava, rich in iron and magnesium. It weathers into fertile, dark soils that retain heat. Basalt is important in Oregon (Jory soils), Washington's Columbia Valley, Soave Classico's eastern hills, Hungary's Badacsony and Somló, and Victoria's Heathcote. Wines from basalt are often described as dense and smoky.

Stirring the lees in a barrel or tank with a stick (bâton) to put the dead yeast cells back into suspension. The process enriches the wine with mannoproteins and polysaccharides, giving creamier texture and roundness, and helps prevent reductive aromas. It is classic in white Burgundy, especially Meursault, and in some Champagne base wines. Too much stirring can make wines heavy and dull their fruit, so many producers now use it sparingly.

A wine region south of Burgundy, on granite and schist hills, devoted almost entirely to Gamay. It has a basic appellation, Beaujolais-Villages and ten crus (Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly). Semi-carbonic maceration gives its fruity style. Beaujolais Nouveau, released on the third Thursday of November since 1985, once accounted for a huge share of production.

Literally 'berry selection', a Prädikat level for wines made from individually selected overripe berries, usually affected by noble rot. BA wines are lusciously sweet, low in alcohol and rare, made only in exceptional years. In Austria, Burgenland's Neusiedlersee produces BA almost every year thanks to autumn mists from the lake. Minimum must weights vary by region but are typically above 110 to 128 degrees Oechsle.

The authorisation that sets how much Port each Douro vineyard may produce each year. Vineyards are graded A to F on a points system that has existed since 1947, considering altitude, yield, soil, slope, exposure, vine age and other factors. The higher the grade, the larger the share of a vineyard's grapes that may be fortified into Port. The rest becomes dry Douro wine. The system protects Port prices but has been criticised for favouring established estates.

A district within a German wine region (Anbaugebiet), such as Bereich Bernkastel in the Mosel or Bereich Johannisberg in the Rheingau. A Bereich wine can come from anywhere in the district, so it is usually basic quality. Germany has 13 Anbaugebiete and about 40 Bereiche. The 2021 law kept them but placed more emphasis on smaller origins.

A farming approach based on Rudolf Steiner's 1924 lectures, treating the vineyard as a self-sustaining organism. Growers use special preparations (such as cow-horn manure, preparation 500, and silica, 501), compost and herbal teas, and time work by lunar and astral calendars. Certification is by Demeter or Biodyvin. Practitioners include Domaine Leroy, Leflaive, Nicolas Joly and Zind-Humbrecht. Scientists are sceptical of some methods, but many growers report healthier soils.

The flat, round, flagon-shaped bottle traditionally used in Franken, protected by EU law for wines from Franken and a few areas of Baden. Its shape is said to come from the pouches travellers once carried. Silvaner and Müller-Thurgau from Franken's shell limestone soils are most often bottled in it. A slightly modernised version was introduced in the 2010s. Portuguese Mateus Rosé uses a similar shape.

A fungicide of copper sulphate and lime (bouillie bordelaise), developed by Professor Pierre-Marie-Alexis Millardet in the Médoc in 1882 to 1885, after he noticed that vines sprayed by growers to deter grape thieves were free of downy mildew. It was the world's first widely used fungicide and is still permitted in organic viticulture, though the EU now limits copper to an average of 4 kg per hectare per year because of soil toxicity.

Botrytis cinerea, a fungus that can either ruin grapes (grey rot) or concentrate them (noble rot), depending on conditions. Noble rot develops when misty mornings are followed by sunny, dry afternoons: the fungus pierces the skins, water evaporates, and sugar, acid and glycerol concentrate. It also creates new flavour compounds, giving honey, apricot, saffron and marmalade notes. It is behind Sauternes, Tokaji Aszú, German TBA and Austrian Ausbruch.

A yeast genus, often shortened to Brett, that can grow in wine and produce volatile phenols (4-ethylphenol and 4-ethylguaiacol) smelling of leather, barnyard, smoked meat or plaster. At low levels some find it adds complexity, and some classic Rhône and Bordeaux wines of the past showed it. At high levels it masks fruit and is considered a fault. Good cellar hygiene and sulphur management control it.

A hardened layer of calcium carbonate that forms in arid and semi-arid soils, binding gravel, sand and clay into a cement-like crust below the surface. It is common in Paso Robles, West Texas, Argentina and parts of Spain and Australia. Roots must find fissures to penetrate it, which limits vigour. Some growers break it with heavy equipment before planting.

Madeira's traditional method of ageing wine in casks stacked on wooden beams (canteiros) in warm lofts, slowly heated by the sun for years. It is required for vintage (frasqueira) Madeira, which must age at least 20 years in cask, and is used for most colheita and 10-year-plus blends. It gives more finesse and complexity than the faster estufagem method.

A fermentation method in which whole, uncrushed bunches are sealed in a tank filled with carbon dioxide. Without oxygen, enzymes inside each berry start fermenting the sugar, producing about 2 percent alcohol and fruity aromas of banana, bubblegum and cherry, before the berries burst. It gives soft, low-tannin, fruity reds, classically Beaujolais Nouveau. Semi-carbonic maceration, with some crushed grapes at the bottom, is more common, and Michel Flanzy studied the method scientifically in the 1930s.

In Georgian winemaking, the mass of skins, stems and seeds that ferments with the juice in a qvevri; also the name for the grape-pomace brandy distilled from it. The proportion of chacha left in the qvevri determines how tannic and amber a white wine becomes. Kakhetian tradition uses full chacha, while western Georgian (Imeretian) tradition uses only a small amount.

A soft, white, porous form of limestone made of coccolith skeletons from the Cretaceous seas, about 70 to 100 million years old. It holds up to 40 percent water, releasing it to roots in dry periods, and reflects heat and light. It underlies Champagne, England's South Downs, Jerez (as albariza, chalky marl) and parts of the Loire. The Champagne houses' cellars are carved into it.

Adding sugar to grape must before or during fermentation to increase the final alcohol, named after Jean-Antoine Chaptal, Napoleon's interior minister, who promoted it in 1801. It is allowed within limits in cooler EU regions such as northern France, Germany and England, but banned in Italy, Spain, Portugal and California, and for German Prädikatswein. Warmer vintages have made it less necessary, and acidification is now more common.

Making sparkling wine with the second fermentation in a sealed pressure tank (autoclave), then bottling under pressure. It is cheaper and quicker than the traditional method and preserves fresh, fruity aromas. It is used for Prosecco, Asti and Lambrusco. It was patented by Federico Martinotti in Italy in 1895 and developed by Eugène Charmat in France in 1907, so Italians call it Martinotti method.

A wine estate, especially in Bordeaux, where the term may be used on labels only for wine from a defined property with its own vineyards and winemaking. Many 'châteaux' are simple farmhouses. The château system, in which an estate's name rather than its vineyards carries the reputation, began with Haut-Brion in the 17th century and was entrenched by the 1855 classification. Owners can buy or sell vineyard land and keep the name.

The squat 62 cl bottle used for Jura vin jaune, said to represent the volume remaining from one litre of wine after six years and three months of ageing under voile, when evaporation (the angel's share) has taken about 38 percent. It is legally reserved for vin jaune. Its origin as a name is uncertain, and its use is protected for Jura wines.

In Burgundy, a precisely delimited, named vineyard plot recognised for centuries for its particular soil, exposure and microclimate. There are 1,247 climats in the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune, ranging from grand crus such as Chambertin to modest village plots. They were inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2015. A climat can contain several lieux-dits, and a lieu-dit can include parts of several climats.

A vineyard enclosed by walls, historically built by monasteries or nobles to protect vines from animals and thieves and to mark ownership. Walls can also create a warmer microclimate. Famous examples include the Clos de Vougeot (about 50 hectares, walled by 1336), Clos de Tart and Clos des Lambrays in Burgundy, and Krug's Clos du Mesnil in Champagne. On labels, 'clos' should refer to a genuinely enclosed or historic site.

Portuguese for 'harvest', used for tawny Port and Madeira from a single vintage. Colheita Port must age at least seven years in wood before bottling and shows the date. Colheita Madeira must spend at least five years in cask. The term gives vintage dating to wood-aged styles, unlike vintage Port, which ages mainly in bottle.

The difference between average temperatures of the warmest and coldest months, reflecting distance from the sea. Highly continental regions, such as Germany, Austria, Hungary, Ningxia or Washington's Columbia Valley, have hot summers and cold winters, sometimes cold enough to kill vines. Maritime regions, such as Bordeaux or New Zealand's Marlborough, are milder. In China and Russia growers bury vines in winter to protect them.

A collective brand formed in 2015 by a group of top Penedès sparkling wine producers who left the Cava DO in 2019 to set stricter rules. Corpinnat wines must be organic, hand-harvested, made entirely on the estate, from at least 90 percent native varieties (Xarel·lo, Macabeo, Parellada) and aged at least 18 months. Members include Gramona, Recaredo and Llopart. It has been recognised by the EU as a private collective brand rather than a PDO.

A disorder in which flowers fail to set fruit, so bunches have few berries. It is caused by cold, wet weather or imbalance around flowering. Grenache, Merlot and Malbec are particularly prone. Millerandage is a related condition in which berries of different sizes develop in the same bunch, often called 'hens and chicks', which can reduce yield but improve concentration.

Ancient chalk pits dug beneath Reims, many by the Romans from the 3rd and 4th centuries AD, to quarry chalk blocks for building. Champagne houses such as Ruinart, Taittinger, Veuve Clicquot and Pommery converted them into cellars, which keep a constant temperature of about 10 to 12 degrees Celsius. Some descend more than 30 metres. They were listed by UNESCO in 2015 as part of the Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars.

Literally 'nursery', one of the younger tiers of barrels in a sherry solera system. A fino solera may have three to nine criaderas, each slightly older than the last. Wine moves from the youngest criadera through the older ones to the solera, so it ages gradually and the flor yeast is constantly fed with fresh wine. The structure keeps the house style consistent from year to year.

A Spanish ageing category for red wine aged at least two years, with at least six months in oak (12 months in Rioja and Ribera del Duero), before release. Reserva requires three years with at least one in oak, and Gran Reserva five years with at least 18 months in oak (in Rioja, at least two years in barrel and two in bottle). The terms emphasise time, not place, a philosophy now shifting toward vineyard categories.

Literally 'growth', meaning a vineyard or estate recognised for quality. Its meaning varies by region: in Burgundy it applies to vineyards (premier cru, grand cru); in Bordeaux to châteaux (the 1855 crus classés); in Beaujolais to ten villages; in Champagne to whole villages rated on the old échelle des crus. Italian and Spanish producers also use the word informally for single vineyards. It always implies a place with a reputation.

A classified growth: an estate ranked in an official classification. In Bordeaux this means the 1855 Médoc and Sauternes ranking, the Graves classification (1953, revised 1959) and the Saint-Émilion classification revised roughly every ten years (most recently 2022). Provence has 18 crus classés from 1955. Unlike Burgundy's vineyard-based crus, Bordeaux classifies châteaux, which can buy or sell land and keep their rank.

Freezing grapes artificially before pressing to remove water as ice and concentrate the juice, imitating icewine or noble rot. It was used in Sauternes in difficult vintages such as 1987, and is permitted within limits. Canadian law forbids wines made this way from being called icewine. Critics call it a shortcut, while defenders see it as a tool for saving crops in wet years.

Districtus Austriae Controllatus, Austria's appellation system, introduced in 2003 with Weinviertel DAC (Grüner Veltliner). Each DAC defines a typical regional style, usually tied to one or two grapes, with a three-tier pyramid of regional, village (Ortswein) and single vineyard (Riedenwein). Austria now has 18 DACs, including Kamptal, Kremstal, Wachau (2020) and Leithaberg. DAC wines must pass a tasting panel.

Slate from the Devonian period, about 400 million years ago, which forms the steep slopes of Germany's Mosel, Saar, Ruwer, Ahr and Middle Rhine. Blue-grey slate dominates around Bernkastel and Wehlen, while red slate occurs in the Ürziger Würzgarten and Erdener Prälat. Growers and critics often distinguish the flavours of wines from different slate types, though the science is debated.

Removing the yeast sediment from a sparkling wine bottle after riddling (French dégorgement). The neck is frozen in brine, the crown cap removed, and pressure pushes out the frozen plug of yeast. Dosage is added and the bottle is corked. Late-disgorged wines (Bollinger's R.D. was a pioneer) spend extra years on lees for complexity. Some producers now print the disgorgement date on the back label.

The difference between daytime high and night-time low temperatures (diurnal temperature variation). A large diurnal range, common at high altitude or in continental and desert climates, helps grapes keep acidity and aromatic compounds while sugars accumulate in the day. Mendoza, Salta, Ningxia and Washington State are examples, with differences of 15 to 20 degrees Celsius. Fog and ocean breezes create similar effects in coastal California and Chile.

Denominación de Origen, Spain's main appellation category, regulated by a consejo regulador (governing council) for each region. Rioja was the first in 1925 and was formally constituted in 1926. Spain has about 70 DOs, from Rías Baixas to Jerez. Above DO sits DOCa (Rioja and Priorat, called DOQ in Catalan), and Vinos de Pago for single estates. The Spanish system emphasises ageing categories more than vineyards.

Denominazione di Origine Controllata, Italy's main appellation category, created by a 1963 law; the first DOC was Vernaccia di San Gimignano in 1966. Italy has more than 330 DOCs. In Portugal, DOC (Denominação de Origem Controlada) is the equivalent top category, used for regions such as the Douro, Dão and Vinho Verde. Both are now PDOs under EU law.

Denominación de Origen Calificada, Spain's highest regional category, given only to Rioja (1991) and Priorat (DOQ, Denominació d'Origen Qualificada in Catalan: approved by the Catalan government in 2000, confirmed nationally in 2009). It requires a long track record of quality, higher grape prices than average and stricter controls, such as bottling within the region. In 2017 Rioja added categories for municipalities, zones (Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa, Rioja Oriental) and single vineyards (viñedos singulares).

Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, Italy's top category, created by the 1963 law and first awarded in 1980 to Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, Barolo and Barbaresco. Wines must pass a tasting panel and carry a numbered government seal on the neck. Italy has close to 80 DOCGs; critics say some were promoted for political reasons rather than quality. A DOC must normally exist for at least seven years before being promoted to DOCG.

In Burgundy and much of France, an estate that grows its own grapes and makes and bottles its own wine, as opposed to a négociant. Domaine bottling took off in Burgundy in the 1930s, when Raymond Baudoin and the importer Frank Schoonmaker persuaded growers such as Henri Gouges and Armand Rousseau to bottle their own wine. Today the top Burgundies mostly come from domaines.

The small amount of sugar solution (liqueur d'expédition, usually wine and cane sugar) added to sparkling wine after disgorgement, determining its sweetness. Labels indicate the level: brut nature or zero dosage (under 3 grams per litre, no sugar added), extra brut (up to 6), brut (up to 12), extra dry (12 to 17), sec (17 to 32), demi-sec (32 to 50) and doux (over 50). Lower dosages have become fashionable as warmer vintages give riper grapes.

Plasmopara viticola, a water mould from North America that attacks leaves, shoots and berries in warm, wet weather, causing yellow oil spots on leaves and white downy growth underneath. It reached France in 1878 and caused severe losses in the 1880s. Bordeaux mixture, a copper-lime spray, was developed in 1885 to control it. Wet vintages such as 2018 and 2023 in Bordeaux and 2024 in parts of Europe showed it remains a major threat.

Growing vines without irrigation, relying on rain and soil moisture. It is the norm in most of Europe and is common among old-vine and quality growers in California, where vines are often widely spaced and head-trained. Dry-farmed vines develop deep roots and smaller berries, which some argue gives more concentrated, site-expressive wine. EU appellations often restrict irrigation, though climate change has led to some relaxations.

The former 'ladder of growths' that rated each Champagne village from 80 to 100 percent and set the price paid for its grapes. Villages at 100 percent were grand cru (17 villages), 90 to 99 percent premier cru (42 villages). The fixed pricing system ended in 1990 and the scale itself was dropped in the 2000s, but grand cru and premier cru remain as village labels. It explains why Champagne classifies whole villages rather than single vineyards.

A single vineyard site registered under German wine law. The 1971 law merged around 30,000 historic sites into about 2,600 Einzellagen, many of them enlarged far beyond their historic boundaries, which diluted the meaning of famous names. Several Einzellagen form a Grosslage. Labels such as Bernkasteler Doctor show the village name (with the suffix -er) plus the Einzellage.

Ice wine, made from grapes frozen naturally on the vine and pressed while frozen, so that water remains as ice and only concentrated juice flows. German law requires harvest at minus 7 degrees Celsius or below; Canada's VQA requires minus 8. Warmer winters have made German Eiswein increasingly rare, with some vintages producing none. Canada, especially Ontario with Vidal and Riesling, is now the largest producer.

Selling wine as futures, before it is bottled. In Bordeaux each spring, châteaux release a portion of the previous vintage at an opening price through the place de Bordeaux, and buyers pay a year or more before delivery. Burgundy, the Rhône and Port also sell this way. The system finances producers and once offered buyers lower prices, but rising release prices and the slump of the 2020s weakened it.

Literally 'raw' or 'from the branch', a sherry (usually fino or manzanilla) bottled straight from the barrel with little or no filtration or cold stabilisation. It preserves more flavour and texture from the flor. Until the late 20th century this was how sherry was drunk locally. Producers such as Tío Pepe and Barbadillo now release en rama bottlings each spring, when flor is thickest.

The second tier of the VDP vineyard pyramid, roughly equivalent to Burgundy's premier cru, below Grosse Lage. Germany's 2021 wine law adopted Erste Lage as an official category for regional protection associations to use. Austria's growers adopted the term Erste Lage (1ÖTW) for their own classification of single vineyards in the Kamptal, Kremstal, Traisental, Wagram and Thermenregion.

Madeira's method of heating wine in a stainless steel or concrete tank (estufa) to about 45 to 50 degrees Celsius for at least three months, replicating the effect of long tropical sea voyages that gave the wine its character in the 18th century. It is used for most standard Madeira, mainly from Tinta Negra. After heating, the wine rests before ageing in cask. Better wines use the slower canteiro method.

The rarest Tokaji: the free-run juice that trickles from aszú berries under their own weight before pressing. It often contains more than 450 grams per litre of sugar (some reach over 800) and ferments so slowly that it may reach only 2 to 5 percent alcohol after years. It is traditionally served by the spoonful and was considered a medicine at European courts. It can age for centuries.

The middle category of Vinea Wachau's three-tier system for dry wines, with 11.5 to 12.5 percent alcohol. The name refers to a falconry lure, a reference to the region's hunting tradition. Federspiel wines are elegant and fresh, often seen by locals as the best expression of the Wachau's mineral style. They are bottled in spring after harvest and can age well.

A layer of yeast (mainly Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains) that forms on the surface of wine in partly filled barrels, protecting it from oxygen and consuming alcohol, glycerol and acids while producing acetaldehyde, which gives fino and manzanilla their tangy, nutty, salty character. Flor thrives in the humid, mild air of Sanlúcar and Jerez and at about 15 to 15.5 percent alcohol. The Jura's vin jaune relies on a similar film called the voile.

Wine to which distilled grape spirit has been added, raising alcohol to about 15 to 22 percent. Adding spirit during fermentation (mutage) leaves sugar, as in Port, Madeira, Vins Doux Naturels and Marsala; adding it after fermentation gives dry styles, as in fino and oloroso sherry. Fortification began as a way to stabilise wine for long sea voyages, and Britain was its key market.

A crumbly, flaky schistous clay-marl soil common in the Chianti Classico hills and parts of Montalcino. It is grey to reddish-brown, breaks into small plates, and drains well, forcing vine roots deep. Many growers associate it with perfumed, structured, finely tannic Sangiovese, and it is prized at estates such as Castello di Ama and in Gaiole and Radda. It is often found with alberese, a harder limestone.

Large, rounded quartzite pebbles carried down by the ancient Rhône and deposited on terraces in the southern Rhône, famously at Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Lirac. They absorb heat in the day and release it at night, helping Grenache ripen fully, and they reduce evaporation from the soil. Not all of Châteauneuf has galets; sand and limestone soils produce more delicate styles, as at Château Rayas.

A term coined in the 1990s for small-scale Bordeaux producers making concentrated wines in tiny quantities, some literally in garages. Jean-Luc Thunevin's Château de Valandraud in Saint-Émilion, first made in 1991, was the archetype, and Le Pin in Pomerol was an earlier forerunner. Garage wines challenged the established hierarchy and won high scores. Valandraud was promoted to premier grand cru classé in 2012.

Geographical Indication, the term used in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa (as Wine of Origin) and in international trade law for a protected place name. Australia's GIs, set by Wine Australia since 1993, form a hierarchy of zones, regions and subregions, such as Barossa Zone, Barossa Valley and Eden Valley. They define boundaries only. A wine labelled with a GI must contain at least 85 percent grapes from that area.

An area of about 800 hectares in Hawke's Bay, New Zealand, defined by a soil type: stony alluvial gravels laid down by the Ngaruroro River, which changed course after a flood in 1867. Once considered worthless land, it was planted from the 1980s, and the Gimblett Gravels Winegrowers Association trademarked the name in 2001. It produces some of New Zealand's best Syrah and Bordeaux blends.

A metamorphic rock formed from granite or sediment under high heat and pressure, with distinctive light and dark bands. It underlies the steep Wachau terraces in Austria, including the Kellerberg and Loibenberg, as well as parts of the Kremstal and Muscadet. It weathers slowly into shallow, stony soils. Riesling and Grüner Veltliner from gneiss are often described as tense and stony.

An old Tuscan technique, the governo all'uso toscano, in which a small portion of grapes is dried and then added, crushed, to a fermented wine to start a second fermentation. It adds softness, fruitiness, a slight sparkle and stability. It was common in Chianti in the 19th century and was mentioned by Ricasoli; a few producers still use it, mainly for early-drinking wines.

The top category of Chianti Classico, introduced in 2014, above Riserva and Annata. It requires estate-grown grapes, at least 30 months of ageing and, under the 2021 reform (compulsory from the 2027 vintage), at least 90 percent Sangiovese with only native varieties as the rest. From the 2020s it may carry one of 11 UGA village names. Critics initially saw it as a marketing tier, but the reforms have made it a serious statement of site.

The highest vineyard category in Burgundy, Alsace and Champagne, though each region uses it differently. Burgundy has 33 grand crus, each its own appellation, such as Montrachet and Romanée-Conti, together about 1 to 2 percent of production. Alsace has 51 grands crus, named on labels with the variety. In Champagne, 17 villages hold grand cru status. In Saint-Émilion, 'grand cru' is a broad appellation and the classified estates use 'grand cru classé'.

A hard igneous rock of quartz, feldspar and mica that weathers into coarse, sandy, acidic soils (gore in Beaujolais) that drain well and are low in nutrients. It underlies Beaujolais crus such as Fleurie, Chiroubles and Moulin-à-Vent, the northern Rhône (Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie's Côte Blonde, Cornas), Muscadet, Swartland, Dão and parts of Galicia and Corsica. Wines from granite are often aromatic and elegant.

Coarse, rounded stones and sand deposited by rivers, which drain freely and warm quickly. The Médoc's gravel ridges (croupes), deposited by the ancestral Garonne and Dordogne, are home to the 1855 classified growths, especially in Pauillac and Margaux, where Cabernet Sauvignon ripens best. Graves takes its name from them. Gravel also defines Hawke's Bay's Gimblett Gravels and parts of the Rhône.

Removing unripe bunches during the growing season, usually around véraison, to reduce yields and concentrate the vine's resources on the remaining fruit (French vendange verte). It became popular in the 1990s in Bordeaux and elsewhere. The EU also uses green harvesting as a crisis measure, paying growers to remove fruit to avoid surpluses, as in the 2020s Bordeaux and Languedoc crises.

The top vineyard category of the VDP (Verband Deutscher Prädikatsweingüter), the German growers' association, roughly equivalent to Burgundy's grand cru. Dry wines from a Grosse Lage are labelled Grosses Gewächs (GG). The VDP's pyramid (Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage, Grosse Lage) was introduced in stages from 2002 and finalised in 2012, and Germany's 2021 wine law adopted a similar origin-based structure. Examples include Wehlener Sonnenuhr and Forster Kirchenstück.

Literally 'great growth', the VDP term for dry wines from Grosse Lage vineyards, marked GG on the label and in an embossed bottle. They are released no earlier than September of the year after harvest (reds two years later). GG Rieslings from the Pfalz, Rheingau, Nahe and Mosel compete with the best dry whites in the world. The term is a private association mark, not a legal category, and sweet wines from the same sites keep traditional Prädikat names.

A collective site under German wine law, grouping several Einzellagen, created by the 1971 law. Grosslage names (such as Piesporter Michelsberg or Niersteiner Gutes Domtal) look like single vineyards on labels, which has misled consumers into thinking cheap blends came from specific sites. The 2021 law requires Grosslage wines to be labelled as Region, and their use is being phased out.

A measure of accumulated heat during the growing season, calculated by adding each day's mean temperature above a base (usually 10 degrees Celsius, below which vines barely grow). It is the basis of the Winkler index. Cool-climate regions accumulate around 1,000 to 1,400 GDD (Celsius), hot regions over 2,200. Climate change has raised GDD across most wine regions, shifting many up a Winkler class since the 1980s.

A vine trained as a freestanding bush, without a trellis, with short spurs arranged around the top of a trunk (Spanish en vaso, French gobelet, Italian alberello). It is traditional in hot, dry Mediterranean regions because the canopy shades the fruit and the low, wide spacing suits dry farming. Many old Grenache, Carignan, Zinfandel and Mourvèdre vineyards are head-trained, and it is hard to mechanise.

A heliothermal index developed by the French scientist Pierre Huglin in 1978. It sums daily temperatures (using mean and maximum) above 10 degrees Celsius from April to September, with a correction for latitude and day length. It is preferred in Europe because it accounts for daytime warmth during the ripening period. Values range from about 1,500 (cool, suitable for Müller-Thurgau) to over 3,000 (very warm).

The Canadian term (trademarked by VQA) for wine made from grapes naturally frozen on the vine at minus 8 degrees Celsius or colder and pressed frozen. Canada, especially the Niagara Peninsula, is the world's largest producer, using Vidal, Riesling and Cabernet Franc. Inniskillin's 1989 Vidal Icewine won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in 1991. Imitations made by freezing grapes artificially (cryoextraction) cannot use the name in Canada.

Indicazione Geografica Tipica, Italy's regional wine category, created in 1992 and now equivalent to the EU PGI (also labelled IGP). It allows non-traditional varieties and blends, so many Super Tuscans and other rule-breaking wines carry it, such as Toscana IGT. It sits between basic Vino and DOC. Many top producers use it deliberately to avoid restrictive DOC rules on grapes, ageing or yields.

Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité, the French public body that defines and controls appellations of origin. Founded in 1935 as the Comité National des Appellations d'Origine and renamed in 1947, it was given authority over cheeses and other products later. Each appellation's rules (cahier des charges) are drafted by growers' unions and approved by the INAO. It also maps parcel boundaries, which form the official delimitations used on maps.

A deep, red, iron-rich clay loam formed from weathered Columbia River basalt, the official state soil of Oregon since 2011. It dominates the Dundee Hills, where pioneers such as David Lett (The Eyrie Vineyards) and Domaine Drouhin planted Pinot Noir. It drains well but holds some water, and Pinot from Jory soils is often described as red-fruited and silky. It contrasts with marine sedimentary soils such as Willakenzie.

The lightest Prädikat level in German wine, from fully ripe grapes picked at normal harvest time, usually low in alcohol (often 7.5 to 10 percent for sweet versions). Classic Mosel Kabinett is delicate, off-dry and racy. The name may come from the 'cabinet' cellar at Kloster Eberbach, where reserve wines were stored in the 18th century. Warmer vintages have made true light Kabinett harder to produce, and some growers now pick early specifically for it.

The Armenian term for a large clay jar used for fermenting and storing wine, similar to the Georgian qvevri, sometimes buried in the ground. Karases have been found at Areni-1, where the world's oldest winery dates to about 4100 BC. Armenian producers such as Zorah revived their use in the 2010s, sourcing old karases from villages and using them for Areni and Voskehat.

A geological stage of the Late Jurassic, about 157 to 152 million years ago, named after Kimmeridge on the Dorset coast. In wine it refers to the limestone-marl soils of Chablis, studded with fossils of the small comma-shaped oyster Exogyra virgula. Kimmeridgian marl also underlies Sancerre and parts of the Aube in Champagne. Chablis grand crus and premiers crus grow on it, and it is credited with the wines' mineral, saline tension.

The basket-shaped training system of Santorini, in which vine canes are coiled into a low ring on the ground, with grapes hanging inside to protect them from the island's strong winds and sun. Every 50 to 100 years, the vine is cut back and a new basket is formed on the same roots, so root systems may be centuries old. It is mostly used for Assyrtiko, Athiri and Aidani.

A shallow stone or granite tank in which grapes are trodden by foot, traditional in the Douro for Port. Teams of treaders work in lines, often to music, crushing the grapes gently without breaking seeds, which extracts colour and tannin quickly before fortification stops fermentation after two or three days. Many top Port houses still use lagares, or robotic versions, for their best wines. Some Douro and Alentejo table-wine producers use them too.

A traditional place name for a small area of land, recorded on the land register (cadastre). In wine it refers to a named vineyard site that is not classified as premier or grand cru. Burgundy and Alsace allow some lieux-dits to appear on labels in smaller type than the appellation, and Champagne and the Loire increasingly use them for single-vineyard wines. The term implies local recognition but no official quality ranking.

Sedimentary rock made mostly of calcium carbonate, often from shells and skeletons of marine organisms. It is the foundation of many great wine regions: Burgundy, Champagne (as chalk), Saint-Émilion, the Loire (tuffeau), Jerez, Coonawarra and Paso Robles. It drains well, holds water in fissures, and is alkaline, which helps keep acidity in grapes. Vines on limestone often need special rootstocks (based on Vitis berlandieri) to avoid chlorosis.

The mixture of wine, sugar (about 24 grams per litre), yeast and nutrients added to still base wine before bottling to trigger the second fermentation in the traditional method. The fermentation produces about 1.2 to 1.3 percent more alcohol and carbon dioxide, building pressure of about 6 atmospheres. The bottle is sealed with a crown cap and the wine ages on its lees (sur lattes).

The dark, crumbly slate and schist soil of Priorat in Catalonia, sparkling with mica and quartz. Formed in the Palaeozoic era, it is poor in nutrients and holds little water, so vines struggle and yields are tiny. Roots dig deep through fractures. It gives Priorat's Garnacha and Cariñena their concentration and mineral, graphite-like character. René Barbier, Álvaro Palacios and others revived the region in the late 1980s on these slopes.

A wind-blown, silty sediment deposited during the ice ages, yellow to buff and rich in calcium. It forms deep, fertile soils that hold water but drain well. It is important in Austria's Wagram, Kremstal and Weinviertel, Germany's Kaiserstuhl, Rheinhessen and Pfalz, Hungary and China, and also in the Columbia Valley in Washington. Grüner Veltliner on loess is typically fruity, spicy and full-bodied.

A secondary conversion in which lactic acid bacteria (usually Oenococcus oeni) turn sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, lowering acidity and adding buttery notes from diacetyl. Almost all red wines go through it. In whites, it is a stylistic choice: common in white Burgundy and Californian Chardonnay, often blocked in Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc and some Champagnes to keep freshness. It was understood scientifically only in the 20th century.

A fino-style sherry made and aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda at the mouth of the Guadalquivir. The town's humid, cool, sea-breezy climate keeps the flor thick all year, so manzanilla is lighter, fresher and saltier than Jerez fino. Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda is its own DO. Manzanilla pasada is an older version where the flor has begun to fade.

A soil or sedimentary rock of mixed clay and calcium carbonate, typically 35 to 65 percent carbonate. Marls hold moisture better than pure limestone and are found in many great vineyards: Kimmeridgian marl in Chablis, the Tortonian and Serravallian marls of Barolo, the marly limestone of the Côte d'Or, and albariza in Jerez. They often give wines with structure and acidity.

The ancestral method of making sparkling wine by bottling before the first fermentation ends, so that bubbles form from the remaining sugar. Limoux in the Languedoc claims records from 1531 for Blanquette de Limoux, while Clairette de Die and Bugey Cerdon use it today for sweet, low-alcohol sparkling wines. It is the technical basis of modern pét-nat.

The traditional method of making sparkling wine with a second fermentation in the bottle, used for Champagne, Cava, Franciacorta, Crémant, English sparkling wine and many others. After the tirage, wines age on lees, are riddled, disgorged and dosed. Champagne requires at least 15 months on lees for non-vintage wine and 36 for vintage. The method was known as méthode champenoise until the EU restricted that term to Champagne in 1994.

A family of compounds, notably IBMP (3-isobutyl-2-methoxypyrazine), giving green pepper, grass and leaf aromas to Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Carmenère. Humans can detect them at a few parts per trillion. Sunlight on the bunches breaks them down, so leaf removal and riper picking reduce them. They help define Sauvignon Blanc's style, but excess in red wines is seen as a fault.

Menzione Geografica Aggiuntiva, an 'additional geographical mention': officially defined vineyard areas within an Italian DOCG that can appear on labels. Barbaresco defined 66 MGAs in 2007 and Barolo 181 in 2010, including Cannubi, Brunate and Vigna Rionda. MGAs are geographical, not ranked by quality, but they make it possible to compare sites, as Burgundy does with its climats. Other regions, such as Soave and Roero, have followed.

Uneven fruit set, producing bunches with a mix of large, normal berries and small, seedless ones (also called 'hens and chicks'). It is caused by poor weather during flowering or nutrient deficiencies. It lowers yields but can raise quality because the small berries have higher skin-to-juice ratios. Some Chardonnay clones from the Mendoza clone family are known for it.

A widely used but disputed tasting term for wines that taste of stone, chalk, flint, slate or salt rather than fruit. Scientists point out that vines do not absorb rock flavours directly; the impression may come from acidity, reductive sulphur compounds, low fruitiness or saline compounds. Still, tasters consistently use it for wines from places like Chablis, the Mosel and Santorini. Many prefer more specific terms such as 'saline' or 'flinty'.

A series of huge floods that swept across eastern Washington and northern Oregon at the end of the last ice age, between about 18,000 and 15,000 years ago, when ice dams holding back glacial Lake Missoula repeatedly broke. They deposited sand, silt and gravel across the Columbia Basin, forming the soils of Walla Walla, Red Mountain and much of the Columbia Valley, and scoured the Columbia River Gorge.

A vineyard or appellation owned entirely by a single producer. In Burgundy, where most vineyards are divided among many growers after centuries of inheritance and the Napoleonic Code, monopoles are rare and prized: Romanée-Conti and La Tâche (Domaine de la Romanée-Conti), Clos de Tart and La Grande Rue are examples. Château-Grillet in the northern Rhône is a single-owner AOC. A monopole lets one producer's style define the site.

The white wine of the Pays Nantais at the western end of the Loire, made from Melon de Bourgogne, which replaced older vines after the great frost of 1709. The best appellation, Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, often ages sur lie. Since 2011 crus communaux such as Clisson, Gorges and Le Pallet require long lees ageing and show the influence of granite, gneiss and gabbro. It is the classic partner for oysters.

Stopping fermentation by adding grape spirit (usually about 77 percent alcohol for Port), which kills the yeasts, leaving natural grape sugar and raising alcohol to about 15 to 22 percent. It is the method behind Port, Madeira, Vins Doux Naturels (Banyuls, Maury, Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise) and some sherries. Timing determines sweetness: earlier mutage leaves more sugar.

Wine made with minimal intervention: organic or biodynamic grapes, hand harvesting, wild yeasts, no additives and little or no sulphur dioxide. There was no official definition until France recognised a 'Vin Méthode Nature' label in 2020, which allows up to 30 milligrams per litre of added sulphites. The movement grew from Beaujolais (Jules Chauvet, Marcel Lapierre) and the Loire in the 1980s.

A merchant who buys grapes, must or wine from growers and blends, ages and sells it under their own name. Négociants dominate Champagne and much of Burgundy and Beaujolais, and Bordeaux's place de Bordeaux sells château wines through négociants and courtiers (brokers). Burgundy houses such as Louis Jadot, Joseph Drouhin and Bouchard also own significant vineyards, blurring the line with domaines.

A Champagne producer that buys grapes from growers, as well as using its own, marked 'NM' on labels. Almost all the famous houses, such as Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot and Krug, are NM. They own only about 10 percent of Champagne's 34,000 hectares, buying the rest from about 16,000 growers. Other codes on labels include CM (cooperative) and MA (marque auxiliaire, a buyer's own brand).

The beneficial form of Botrytis cinerea infection that concentrates grapes for sweet wine. French call it pourriture noble, Germans Edelfäule, Hungarians aszúsodás. Rivers and lakes that bring autumn mist are essential: the Ciron and Garonne in Sauternes, the Bodrog and Tisza in Tokaj, Lake Neusiedl in Burgenland. Harvesting requires several passes (tries) through the vineyard to pick only affected berries, making the wines expensive.

Powdery mildew (Erysiphe necator), a fungal disease from North America that covers leaves and berries in a grey-white powder, splitting the fruit. First seen in Europe in 1845 at Margate, it spread through France and the Mediterranean in the 1850s, cutting French production by about three quarters and devastating Madeira. Sulphur dusting, discovered in the 1850s, controls it and is still used today, including on organic vineyards.

Vines of a significant age (French vieilles vignes, German alte Reben), usually yielding fewer, more concentrated grapes. There is no legal definition in most countries, but some regions now set rules: South Africa's Old Vine Project certifies vineyards over 35 years, and Barossa's Old Vine Charter classifies vineyards as Old (35+), Survivor (70+), Centenarian (100+) and Ancestor (125+ years). Old vines are also living records of past varieties.

A sherry style aged oxidatively without flor, fortified to about 17 to 18 percent alcohol after the first classification, which prevents flor from growing. Over years in solera it darkens to amber-mahogany and develops walnut, leather and dried fruit flavours while remaining dry. Very old olorosos (VORS, over 30 years) are intense and concentrated. Sweetened versions become cream sherry.

White wine made like a red, fermented with skin contact for days, weeks or months, giving an amber colour, tannin, and flavours of dried fruit, tea and spice. Also called amber or skin-contact wine. Georgia has made it for millennia in qvevri; Friulian and Slovenian producers such as Josko Gravner and Stanko Radikon revived it in Europe in the late 1990s. The British wine merchant David Harvey is credited with coining the term 'orange wine' in 2004.

Topping up barrels to replace wine lost to evaporation, which prevents oxidation. In the Jura, whites made this way are called 'ouillé' or 'floral', a fresher style that has become popular since the 2000s, in contrast to the traditional oxidative and sous voile wines that are deliberately left untopped. Elsewhere, ouillage is standard cellar practice for barrel-aged wines.

Another term for ungrafted vines growing on their own roots (French franc de pied, Spanish pie franco). Own-rooted vines are common in phylloxera-free regions, including Chile, Washington State and the Barossa, and on sandy, volcanic or very cold soils where the aphid struggles. Planting own-rooted vines is cheaper and quicker but risky if phylloxera arrives, as Oregon discovered after it was detected in 1990.

In Jerez and much of southern Spain, a named vineyard district with a recognised character, such as Macharnudo, Miraflores or Añina. Historically, sherry was a blended product, and pagos were almost never named on labels, but a new generation of producers is reviving them to show differences in albariza soil. In wider Spanish law, Vino de Pago refers to single-estate appellations.

The highest tier of Cava, created in 2017 for single vineyards with special soils and climate, requiring at least 36 months on lees, hand harvesting and lower yields. The first 12 were approved in 2017, including Turó d'en Mota (Recaredo) and Can Sala (Freixenet). Cava's 2020 reforms added zoning and stricter ageing, partly in response to the Corpinnat group's departure from the DO in 2019.

Leaving grapes on the vine late into autumn so that they shrivel and dry, concentrating sugars without botrytis. It is used for Jurançon moelleux from Petit Manseng and some Vendanges Tardives in Alsace. Dry autumn winds, such as the foehn in the Pyrenees, help. Some producers twist the stems to stop sap flow and speed drying. Grapes can also be dried on mats or straw (vin de paille).

Italian sweet wine made from dried grapes, whether dried on the vine, on racks or in the sun. Famous examples include Passito di Pantelleria (from Zibibbo), Recioto di Soave, Sagrantino Passito and Vin Santo. The process concentrates sugar, acid and aromatic compounds. Many Italian regions have passito traditions linked to religious festivals, such as Easter or Christmas.

Protected Designation of Origin, the EU's highest category for geographically protected wines, introduced by the 2008 wine reform. A PDO wine must come entirely from grapes grown in the area, made from Vitis vinifera, and have characteristics due to that place. National systems map onto it: French AOC/AOP, Italian DOC and DOCG, Spanish DO and DOCa, Portuguese DOC and German Qualitätswein. PDOs are registered in the EU eAmbrosia database.

Overhead trellising that lifts vines above head height, forming a canopy. It is traditional in Alto Adige and Trentino (pergola trentina), Valpolicella, Galicia (parra) and northern Portugal, where it improves air circulation in wet climates and lets farmers grow crops underneath. Japan's tanazukuri is similar. It shades the fruit, which can help in hot climates but makes mechanisation impossible.

Short for pétillant naturel: sparkling wine made by the ancestral method (méthode ancestrale), bottled before the first fermentation has finished so that the remaining sugar ferments in the bottle and creates bubbles. No liqueur de tirage or dosage is added, and the wine is often left cloudy. It is the oldest sparkling method, traditional in Limoux and Gaillac, and became popular with natural winemakers in the 2010s.

Protected Geographical Indication, the EU category below PDO. At least 85 percent of the grapes must come from the area, and rules on varieties and yields are looser, allowing international varieties and blends across large regions. National equivalents include France's IGP (formerly vin de pays, such as Pays d'Oc), Italy's IGT/IGP and Spain's Vino de la Tierra. Many ambitious wines are sold as PGI to escape restrictive PDO rules.

Daktulosphaira vitifoliae, a tiny aphid-like insect native to North America that feeds on vine roots. American vines evolved tolerance, but European Vitis vinifera roots develop swellings that rot, killing the vine within a few years. Arriving in France around 1863, it destroyed most European vineyards by 1900. The solution was grafting vinifera onto American rootstocks. There is still no cure, and it continues to spread, reaching new areas of Australia and Oregon in recent decades.

The black volcanic lapilli (small cinders) that cover much of Lanzarote in the Canary Islands after the eruptions of 1730 to 1736. In La Geria, farmers dig funnel-shaped hollows (hoyos) through the picón to reach the soil beneath, plant a single vine in each, and protect it with a semicircular stone wall (zoco). The picón traps dew and slows evaporation in a place with almost no rain.

The traditional cask of the Port trade, holding about 550 litres in the Douro and 534.24 litres as a shipping measure in Vila Nova de Gaia. Port is aged in pipes in the cool lodges (armazéns) of Gaia, where the Atlantic climate slows evaporation. Madeira's equivalent is 418 litres. The pipe is also a unit for measuring production and beneficio quotas.

A geological stage of the Late Jurassic (now usually called Tithonian), slightly younger than the Kimmeridgian. In Chablis it forms the hard limestone caps of the plateaus above the Kimmeridgian slopes. Petit Chablis is mostly grown on Portlandian, which is why it was long considered less fine. The distinction between the two soils is central to the Chablis appellation hierarchy.

In German and Austrian wine law, a quality level based on the sugar content of grapes at harvest. The German ladder runs Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese (BA), Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) and Eiswein; Austria adds Strohwein and Ausbruch. Prädikatswein may not be chaptalised. A Prädikat indicates ripeness at harvest, not sweetness in the bottle: a Spätlese can be dry. Terms such as Spätlese and Auslese were in use long before, but the 1971 German law fixed the modern ladder and its definitions.

The second tier of Burgundy's vineyard hierarchy, below grand cru, with about 640 premier cru climats, about 10 percent of production. Labels show the village name plus the vineyard, such as Puligny-Montrachet Les Pucelles. In Bordeaux's 1855 classification, premier cru means first growth, the top level. In Champagne, 42 villages are premier cru, rated 90 to 99 percent on the old échelle des crus.

A light, porous volcanic rock formed from frothy lava. Soils rich in pumice, as on Santorini, Lipari and parts of Campania, drain freely but hold moisture in their pores. They are poor in nutrients and organic matter, keeping yields low. Their sandy texture also keeps phylloxera away, allowing ungrafted vines.

The traditional measure of sweetness in Tokaji Aszú: the number of puttony (hods of about 25 kg of aszú berries) added to a 136 litre gönci barrel of base wine. Labels used to range from 3 to 6 puttonyos. Since a 2013 reform, only the 5 and 6 puttonyos levels remain (at least 120 and 150 grams of sugar per litre), and many producers have dropped the term altogether, simply labelling Tokaji Aszú.

A Portuguese farm or estate, used for wine estates, especially in the Douro, such as Quinta do Noval, Quinta do Vesuvio and Quinta do Crasto. Single-quinta vintage Ports are made from one estate in years not declared as classic vintages, or as estate wines. The idea parallels the Bordeaux château, linking a wine to a single property, and became more common after the 1986 law that allowed Port to be shipped from the Douro rather than Vila Nova de Gaia.

A large egg-shaped clay vessel, usually holding several hundred to a few thousand litres, buried up to its neck in the ground and lined inside with beeswax. In Georgia, crushed grapes, often with skins, stems and seeds (chacha), ferment and age in qvevri sealed for months, producing amber or orange whites and tannic reds. UNESCO inscribed qvevri winemaking as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2013. The tradition is at least 8,000 years old.

A complex, nutty, slightly sour aroma that develops when wines age in oxygen and heat, often in barrels or glass demijohns (bonbonnes) left outside in the sun. It is prized in old Vins Doux Naturels of Banyuls and Rivesaltes, Catalan rancio sec, and old tawny Ports and Madeiras. The flavour recalls walnuts, dried figs, caramel and cheese rind, from compounds such as sotolon.

A sweet wine from the Veneto made from dried grapes (appassimento), whose name comes from recie, dialect for 'ears', the upper lobes of the bunch that get the most sun and ripen best. Recioto della Valpolicella (red, from Corvina) and Recioto di Soave (white, from Garganega) are among Italy's oldest wine styles, likely descended from the Roman acinatico described by Cassiodorus in the 6th century. Amarone began as a Recioto that fermented dry.

A Champagne grower who makes and sells Champagne from their own grapes, marked 'RM' on the label. About 95 percent of the grapes must come from their own vineyards. Grower Champagne, championed by importers such as Terry Theise in the US from the 1990s, offers single-village and single-vineyard expressions, unlike the blended style of the big négociant houses (NM). Pioneers include Anselme Selosse, Pierre Péters and Egly-Ouriet.

Riddling: gradually turning and tilting sparkling wine bottles upside down so that the yeast sediment slides into the neck. Developed by Veuve Clicquot's team in 1816 using pupitres (wooden A-frame racks), it took skilled riddlers about six weeks. Since the 1970s, gyropalettes, machines that move 504 bottles at once, do the same job in about a week. Some houses still riddle prestige cuvées by hand.

In Spain, a red wine aged at least three years before release, with at least one year in oak; whites and rosés need two years. In Portugal, Reserva indicates a wine of superior quality with slightly higher alcohol, approved by a tasting panel. In Chile and Argentina the term has no strict legal meaning beyond minimum alcohol and is widely used for marketing.

In Champagne and other sparkling regions, still wine from earlier harvests kept back to blend into non-vintage cuvées, giving consistency and complexity. Some houses keep them in tanks or barrels; others, like Krug, keep hundreds of reserve wines, and some growers use a perpetual reserve (réserve perpétuelle) refreshed every year like a solera. The share of reserve wine in a blend typically ranges from 10 to over 40 percent.

The Austrian term for a single vineyard site, which must appear as 'Ried' before the name on labels of single-vineyard DAC wines, such as Ried Heiligenstein or Ried Loibenberg. The Österreichische Traditionsweingüter (ÖTW) classify the best Rieden as Erste Lage, and some are being proposed as Grosse Lage. The system emphasises origin rather than ripeness.

A white grape first recorded in 1435 at Rüsselsheim, a child of Gouais Blanc and a Traminer seedling. Known for high acidity, aromatic intensity and transparency to site, it ages for decades and develops a petrol note (TDN). It ranges from bone dry to intensely sweet and dominates the Mosel, Rheingau and Nahe, as well as Alsace, the Wachau, Clare and Eden valleys and the Finger Lakes.

A Valpolicella technique in which young wine is refermented on the dried-grape skins (vinacce) left after pressing Amarone or Recioto. It gains alcohol, body, tannin and some of Amarone's dried-fruit character, earning the nickname 'baby Amarone'. Valpolicella Ripasso became its own DOC in 2010. Masi is often credited with popularising the method in the 1960s with its Campofiorin.

An Italian label term for wine aged longer than the standard version before release, according to each DOC's rules. Barolo Riserva requires 62 months of ageing, Brunello Riserva 6 years, Chianti Classico Riserva 24 months. The Spanish equivalent, Reserva, also signals longer ageing, as does the Portuguese Reserva. It usually implies selected grapes and better vintages, but the legal requirement is about time.

The root system onto which a grape variety is grafted. Since phylloxera, most of the world's vines are grafted onto rootstocks from American species such as Vitis riparia, rupestris and berlandieri, or their crosses (for example 101-14, 3309C, SO4, 41B, 110 Richter, 1103 Paulsen). Rootstocks are chosen for phylloxera resistance, tolerance of lime, drought or salinity, vigour and nematode resistance. They also affect ripening and yield.

A sesquiterpene compound that gives a black and white pepper aroma, identified in Australian Syrah by the Australian Wine Research Institute in 2008. It also occurs in black pepper, Grüner Veltliner, Vespolina, Schioppettino, Duras and Pineau d'Aunis. Cool climates and late ripening increase it. About a fifth of people cannot smell it at all, which helps explain disagreements about peppery wines.

The withdrawal of wine from the oldest tier of a sherry solera for bottling. Legally no more than about a third of each barrel's contents can be removed per year for many styles, so wines spend years in the system. The saca is followed by the rocío, refilling the solera from the first criadera, and so on down the scale.

'Bleeding', the technique of drawing off some pink juice from a tank of red grapes early in maceration. The remaining wine becomes more concentrated, and the juice can be fermented as rosé. It is used in Bordeaux, California and elsewhere. In Champagne, rosé de saignée is made by macerating Pinot Noir briefly, an alternative to the common method of blending red and white wine.

A metamorphic rock with layered, flaky grains, formed when mudstone or shale is heated and pressed. In wine it is found in the Douro, Roussillon (Banyuls, Collioure, Maury), Languedoc (Faugères), Côte-Rôtie, Priorat and Central Otago. Its layers allow roots to penetrate deep in search of water, while the rock absorbs and releases heat. Schist vineyards are usually steep and must be terraced.

Leaving juice in contact with grape skins before or during fermentation (maceration) to extract colour, tannin and aromatic compounds. For red wine it is standard; for white wine, a few hours of pre-fermentation contact can add aroma, while weeks or months produce orange wine. Rosé is made with short skin contact, often a few hours. The length and temperature of maceration are among a winemaker's most important decisions.

A fine-grained metamorphic rock formed from shale, splitting into thin sheets. The Mosel's Devonian slate (about 400 million years old) comes in blue-grey and red forms, and its dark stones hold heat, helping Riesling ripen on steep, south-facing slopes. Slate also defines parts of the Rheingau, Ahr, Priorat (as llicorella), Bierzo and the Loire's Savennières and Anjou. Wines from slate are often described as smoky and mineral.

The richest category of dry Wachau wine, defined by the Vinea Wachau growers' association, founded in 1983. Smaragd wines have at least 12.5 percent alcohol, from the ripest grapes, typically Grüner Veltliner and Riesling from the best terraces. The name comes from the emerald lizard that suns itself on the vineyard walls. Below it come Steinfeder (up to 11.5 percent) and Federspiel (11.5 to 12.5 percent). Chaptalisation and new oak character are not allowed.

A system of fractional blending used for sherry and other wines. Barrels are arranged in tiers: the oldest (the solera) supplies wine for bottling, and the younger tiers (criaderas) refresh it. Only part of each barrel is withdrawn (saca) and replaced from the next-youngest tier (rocío). The wine becomes a blend of many vintages, with a consistent style. Some sherry soleras are said to have been started in the 18th or 19th century.

Literally 'late harvest', the second Prädikat level, from grapes picked at least seven days after the main harvest with higher minimum sugar. The story of its discovery at Schloss Johannisberg in 1775, after a courier delayed the harvest permission, is part of Rheingau folklore. Spätlese can be sweet or dry (Spätlese trocken). In Alsace the equivalent is Vendanges Tardives, and in Austria the term is used similarly.

The lightest Vinea Wachau category, for dry wines up to 11.5 percent alcohol, named after a feathery grass (Stipa pennata) that grows on the dry terraces. Steinfeder wines are light, fresh and meant for early drinking. Warmer vintages have made them rarer, as grapes ripen to higher sugar levels.

A term coined in the 1970s and 1980s for Tuscan red wines made outside the DOC rules, often with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot or 100 percent Sangiovese aged in French barriques. Sassicaia (first commercial vintage 1968) and Tignanello (1971) were pioneers. Because they broke the rules they were sold as humble vino da tavola but at high prices. Later rule changes created Bolgheri DOC (1983) and Toscana IGT (1992) to accommodate them.

Ageing a wine on its fine lees, the dead yeast cells left after fermentation, without racking. Lees contact adds texture, a yeasty or bready flavour and some protection against oxidation. Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie must be bottled straight off its lees after wintering on them, traditionally between March and November of the year after harvest. Many Chardonnays and sparkling wines also benefit from long lees ageing.

A white grape, a child of Traminer and Österreichisch Weiss, once Germany's most planted variety and still the emblem of Franken, where it grows on shell limestone and is bottled in the round Bocksbeutel. In Alsace, Zotzenberg is the only grand cru allowed for Sylvaner. Wines are earthy, herbal and quietly mineral, and excellent with asparagus, a Franconian spring tradition.

A Tokaji style made from whole bunches containing both healthy and botrytised grapes, as they come from the vine. Its name is Polish for 'as it comes'. Sweet (édes) Szamorodni is lightly sweet; dry (száraz) Szamorodni is aged under a flor-like yeast film, giving a style similar to vin jaune or fino sherry. It is an older style than Aszú and has been revived by a number of producers.

A large clay amphora used in Portugal's Alentejo for making Vinho de Talha, a tradition dating back to Roman times. Talhas can hold up to 2,000 litres or more and are lined with pez, a resin coating. Grapes ferment with their skins and the wine is drawn off from a tap near the base, often around Saint Martin's Day (11 November). Vinho de Talha became an official DOC subregion in 2010, centred on Vidigueira.

A style of Port aged in small oak casks (pipes) in Vila Nova de Gaia or the Douro, where oxidation turns the colour tawny-brown and gives nutty, caramel and dried fruit flavours. Aged tawnies carry indications of age (10, 20, 30, 40 and, since 2021, 50 years), describing the average character rather than an exact minimum. Colheita tawnies come from a single year. Ruby Ports, by contrast, are aged briefly and keep their fruit.

2,4,6-Trichloroanisole, the main cause of 'corked' wine, smelling of damp cardboard and mouldy basements and stripping fruit. It forms when fungi interact with chlorinated compounds, typically in cork bark, but also in cellars and barrels. Humans can detect it at a few parts per trillion. In the 1990s a significant share of bottles was affected, which pushed the screwcap movement and better cork processing.

1,1,6-trimethyl-1,2-dihydronaphthalene, the compound responsible for the 'petrol' or kerosene aroma that develops in aged Riesling. It forms from carotenoids in grapes, and its precursors increase with sun exposure, which is why Riesling from sunny Clare and Eden Valley in Australia often develops it quickly. Some love it as a sign of age; others see it as a fault.

Red, clay-rich soil formed by weathering of limestone in Mediterranean and karst regions, coloured by iron oxides. Famously found over limestone in Coonawarra, South Australia, where a strip about 15 km long and under 2 km wide is famous for Cabernet Sauvignon, and in Istria, Puglia and parts of Spain. Its free drainage and the moisture held by the limestone below make it ideal for vines.

The total natural environment of a vineyard (soil, subsoil, slope, aspect, altitude, climate and water supply) together with the human practices that have grown up around it. It explains why wines from neighbouring plots can taste consistently different. The concept underpins the French AOC system and most European appellation laws. Critics argue it is partly marketing, and scientists still debate how soil chemistry affects flavour, but repeated tastings across vintages show that site matters.

A family of sulphur compounds that give passion fruit, grapefruit and blackcurrant aromas, such as 3MH (3-mercaptohexanol), 3MHA and 4MMP. They are released from odourless precursors in the grape during fermentation, especially in Sauvignon Blanc, Scheurebe, Colombard and Gros Manseng. Marlborough's pungent style depends on them, and machine harvesting appears to increase their precursors.

A large clay jar traditionally used in Spain, especially La Mancha, Montilla-Moriles and Valdepeñas, for fermenting and storing wine. Montilla producers still ferment Pedro Ximénez in tinajas before solera ageing. They were made in villages such as Villarrobledo and Colmenar de Oreja, and some old cellars house hundreds. Natural winemakers have revived their use.

Literally 'dried berry selection', the highest German and Austrian Prädikat for wines from shrivelled, botrytised berries picked one by one, with must weights above about 150 degrees Oechsle. Yields can be a few hundred litres per hectare. The wines are intensely sweet, often low in alcohol (6 to 8 percent), with high acidity, and can age for a century. Producers such as Egon Müller and Alois Kracher made their names with TBA.

The Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, the agency of the US Treasury that has regulated wine labelling and approved American Viticultural Areas since 2003, taking over from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms (ATF). Petitions for new AVAs go through the TTB's public rulemaking, and the boundaries are published in the Code of Federal Regulations (27 CFR Part 9). The TTB also approves label designs (COLAs) for all wines sold in the US.

A rock formed from compacted volcanic ash. It is soft enough to carve and porous enough to store water, which made it a popular place to dig cellars, as in Eger in Hungary, Orvieto in Umbria and Tokaj. Campania's Greco di Tufo takes its name from it. Tuff soils are usually light, well drained and rich in minerals. Do not confuse it with tuffeau, the Loire's limestone.

A soft, fine-grained, yellow-white limestone from the Turonian stage of the Cretaceous, found in the Loire valley around Saumur, Vouvray and Chinon. It is porous and holds water, and it is used to build the region's châteaux. Its caves house wineries and mushroom farms. Chenin Blanc and Cabernet Franc from tuffeau slopes are known for finesse and acidity.

How faithfully a wine expresses the expected character of its grape, place and style (French typicité). Appellation tasting panels in France, Italy and Spain can reject wines that lack typicity, which some growers argue penalises unusual or natural wines. A Sancerre should smell of Sauvignon Blanc and taste of chalk and flint; a Barolo should be pale garnet, tannic and perfumed. The idea links terroir to a recognisable style that consumers can trust.

Unità Geografica Aggiuntiva, 'additional geographical unit', the system adopted by Chianti Classico in 2021 to divide its zone into 11 villages or sub-areas, such as Panzano, Radda, Gaiole and Castelnuovo Berardenga. Since the rules took effect in 2023, Gran Selezione wines may show the UGA on the label (Lamole, Montefioralle and Vagliagli only from 2027), including earlier vintages that meet the criteria, and the Gran Selezione rules were tightened to require at least 90 percent Sangiovese from the 2027 vintage. Soave uses the same term for its 33 crus.

Vines grown on their own roots (also own-rooted or franc de pied) rather than grafted onto American rootstocks. They survive where phylloxera is absent, such as Chile, much of South Australia, Cyprus, Santorini and sandy soils such as Colares or Jumilla, or where growers accept the risk. Some winemakers believe ungrafted vines give purer flavours. Bollinger, Quinta do Noval and Mosel growers keep famous ungrafted plots.

Verband Deutscher Prädikatsweingüter, the association of around 200 top German wine estates, founded in 1910 as a group of auction houses. Members' bottles carry an eagle on the capsule. The VDP created its own vineyard classification (Grosse Lage, Erste Lage, Ortswein, Gutswein) and the Grosses Gewächs category, with stricter yields and hand harvesting. It has been more influential than German law in defining quality.

The stage of ripening when grapes change colour, red varieties from green to purple and white ones to translucent yellow-green, and begin to soften and accumulate sugar while acidity falls. In the Northern Hemisphere it usually occurs in July or August, about six to eight weeks before harvest. Growers often thin bunches at véraison (green harvest) to concentrate the remaining fruit and even out ripening.

'Straw wine', a sweet wine made from grapes dried for at least six weeks on straw mats or racks, or hung from rafters, until shrivelled. Traditional in the Jura (from Chardonnay, Savagnin and Poulsard) and Hermitage, it gives rich, honeyed wines with high acidity. In the Jura, it must age at least three years and is sold in half bottles. Austria makes a similar Strohwein.

Naturally sweet fortified wine, often abbreviated VDN, made by mutage: adding neutral spirit to stop fermentation. They come mainly from Roussillon (Banyuls, Maury, Rivesaltes) and the southern Rhône (Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, Rasteau). Red VDNs are often aged oxidatively, sometimes in glass demijohns left in the sun, to develop rancio flavours of walnut and dried fruit. The tradition dates back to Arnaud de Villeneuve, who described mutage in the 13th century.

'Yellow wine' from the Jura, made from Savagnin aged at least six years and three months (from harvest) in barrels that are never topped up. A film of yeast (voile) forms, protecting the wine from oxygen and producing a nutty, curry-like flavour. It is bottled in the 62 cl clavelin, representing what remains of a litre after evaporation. Château-Chalon is its most famous appellation, and the Percée du Vin Jaune festival celebrates each new release.

'Holy wine', a Tuscan dessert wine made from grapes (usually Trebbiano and Malvasia) dried on mats or hung in lofts until winter, then fermented and aged for years in small sealed barrels (caratelli), sometimes with a 'madre', a residue from earlier batches. The barrels sit in attics with hot summers and cold winters, encouraging oxidation. It ranges from dry to very sweet. Vin Santo dell'Occhio di Pernice is made from red grapes.

A 'singular vineyard', a Spanish category created in 2017 for exceptional single vineyards within a DO, with stricter rules: vines at least 35 years old, reduced yields, hand harvesting and tasting approval. Rioja adopted it the same year and has approved dozens; Cava created its own single-vineyard tier, Paraje Calificado, and other DOs have followed with similar categories. It responds to growers' demands to recognise place, not just ageing.

Literally 'wine of the round trip', the name for Madeira that had crossed the equator and returned in the hold of a ship, especially to and from India or the East Indies, in the 18th and 19th centuries.
